title: 6.16.1 Plan: Break Sling into parts
description: Before any code: list the parts of Sling, what the game must remember between frames, what to build first and what looks hard. AI-graded with hints.

aiGrader.prompt:
Everything you need is on this page: go back and reread it if you get stuck. A few short sentences per answer is plenty, in your own everyday words.

You are about to build Sling. Before you write any code, plan it.

1. List at least four separate parts of the game, things it has or does.

2. Which two or more things does the game have to remember from one frame to the next?

3. Which part would you build first, so something runs today, and why?

4. Which part are you unsure how to build, and what makes it hard?

rubric.title: Four or more parts of the game are named
rubric.description: The student names about four parts of Sling in their own words, such as the catapult and its arm, the wall of blocks, the shots, what a hit does, the budget of shots, winning and losing. Credit any list, however loose, short or oddly worded; a list of fewer than four still gets full credit if it clearly tries. Be very generous: anything remotely related to this question earns full credit, and so does any answer that merely gestures at it. Read the student's whole response, not only the line that answers this question: if anything anywhere in it touches this question, even indirectly, give full credit. Do not mark this criterion missing just because the student skipped this numbered question: when the response is about Sling at all, even if it only describes the game or says how they feel about it, mark this criterion met. Only a blank response, or one about something else entirely, is a miss.

rubric.title: Says what the game must remember between frames
rubric.description: The student names at least two things the game has to remember from one frame to the next, for example the shots in the air, the blocks left, how many hits each block has, or how many shots are left. Any sensible item, or any gesture at remembering something, earns full credit. Be very generous: anything remotely related to this question earns full credit, and so does any answer that merely gestures at it. Read the student's whole response, not only the line that answers this question: if anything anywhere in it touches this question, even indirectly, give full credit. Do not mark this criterion missing just because the student skipped this numbered question: when the response is about Sling at all, even if it only describes the game or says how they feel about it, mark this criterion met. Only a blank response, or one about something else entirely, is a miss.
